In the final week, seven days remained until {name}'s thirty-eighth birthday. Beside the notebook where he first wrote KRW 3 billion, he opened the papers from the final month. The label and number he had actually received, the sent time on his notice to Sangchul, and the last empty line came into view together.

Earlier pages held records of the evenings Daeun and Minseo had spent, the sentence aimed at Jaehyuk or kept in {name}'s own ledger, and the action he had taken toward Father. The last line was not a contract. It was where he would place his own name among those lines.

title: The Offer Among Dark Desks
description:
After the closing announcement, the supervisor walked between dark desks. Two people remained because no one had told them who would inherit {name}'s work. He tucked the offer under one arm. “A title is authority the company lends you. Before you climb, tell me who receives the work you leave.”

Tomorrow's executive briefing could open the post, but cost tonight's meal with Hyunsu and an after-midnight handover. Waiting let the team name the time they needed, but the recommendation might vanish. Asking the supervisor to stay borrowed his evening too.

“Being on your side is not living your hours for you.” He stood by the exit without his coat. {name} had to choose who went home, and who remained among the dark desks.

choices.text: Send the remaining team members home and take the handover and executive briefing alone tonight.
choices.result_text:
{name} told both people to shut down their computers. One promised to explain again tomorrow; the other silently packed a bag. The supervisor named the work left at each empty desk and placed the offer on {name}'s desk.

Hyunsu texted that he would wait until the gukbap place closed. {name} opened the first file without answering. The new post moved closer and the team left on time, but the handover and one cooling bowl became his cost for the night.

choices.text: Keep tonight's promise to Hyunsu, hear the team out first, and give the appointment answer tomorrow.
choices.result_text:
The supervisor folded the offer. “The executives may be looking at another name tomorrow. If this is your order, go.” The remaining two people began explaining what sat at their desks.

{name} heard them through, then left for Hyunsu's meal. He kept one person's evening but lost any guarantee that the recommendation would survive. As the elevator closed, the supervisor still held his coat without moving.

choices.text: Ask the supervisor to stay and share the cost of handing over the work he recommended.
choices.result_text:
The supervisor studied {name}, then hung his coat back up. “Fine. But don't call my staying your achievement.” He phoned the executive to say he would be late, then asked each team member what work was leaving whose hands.

The two people departed in turn. The supervisor and {name} remained by the dark window. Rather than rise alone, {name} had borrowed the evening of the man who backed him. The folded offer lay between them, and neither called it a celebration.

title: The Person Who Did Not Wait for the Last Train
description:
Minseo buttoned her coat in the seminar-building lobby. When {name} opened the laptop, she looked at the last-train notice. The company's final call began in twelve minutes; she had to leave now. “You're borrowing my evening again, then asking only for confirmation at the end, aren't you?”

{name} asked what life to protect after the appointment. Minseo shook her head. “If I make that answer, every urgent decision turns my time into your meeting room.” She did not recalculate the offer. She named their agreed meeting, the delayed meal, and the hours {name} kept people before confirmation buttons.

Cold air entered. Minseo was returning to her own night, not serving as his reviewer. The choice remained {name}'s: could he walk beside her without demanding an answer?

choices.text: Close the laptop, walk Minseo to the subway entrance, and let her leave without asking for an answer.
choices.result_text:
{name} silenced the company call and matched Minseo's pace. She neither told him to accept nor refuse. At the subway stairs, she unfolded the life-review sheet {name} had brought. “This is neither approval nor legal review.” She drew a blue line under the twelve-month end date. “It does not approve your decision. It marks the date after which you still need to protect your evenings.” Minseo returned the blue-marked sheet to {name}.

“Next time, don't call me before a decision to obtain my answer. If you call, first tell me whose time you have already used.” By the time she vanished beyond the gates, the company's final call had ended. {name} lost one approval window and received no permission. Minseo kept her remaining evening, while the life-review sheet waited in {name}'s bag for the next room.

title: Four People's Borrowed Evening
description:
At 8:10 p.m., the supervisor, Minseo, and Hyunsu met. {name}'s invitation said, “This is not permission. First I will name whose time I used.” Minseo agreed to thirty minutes before her train.

Before anyone spoke, {name} named Minseo's late dinner, Hyunsu's interrupted night shift and paid time, and the supervisor's delayed call and evening. No one excused him. Only then did Minseo start her timer.

“If friends must authorize this, fold it,” said the supervisor. “Don't use my firm's name to make your decision safe,” Hyunsu said. Minseo added, “Checking figures does not approve his life.” Hyunsu had to resume work in forty minutes; the call was due in twenty. Keeping all three spent their evenings; sending one away meant speaking without them; ending the room risked the recommendation.

choices.text: Send Hyunsu back to work and admit before the other two that his name looked like a shortcut.
choices.result_text:
{name} told Hyunsu to return to night work. Hyunsu stood without thanking him. “Just don't turn my refusal into proof that you made a good decision after I'm gone.” Once the door closed, {name} admitted that he had seen Hyunsu's firm name as ten days saved.

The supervisor told him to state the next action, not a defense. Minseo said the answer Hyunsu deserved remained separate. Hyunsu recovered his time, but {name} lost the chance to hear his full reaction. Only the badge strap receding down the hall remained.

choices.text: Send Minseo to her train and set the company boundary before the supervisor and Hyunsu.
choices.result_text:
Minseo rose, saying, “Don't use my absence as consent.” {name} opened the door before she missed her train. The supervisor then said internal review could proceed without any outside name, and Hyunsu heard directly that his firm would have no part in it.

The boundary became clear, but Minseo's question about life after the goal left unanswered. Only three people appeared in the closed glass door. Her empty chair could not supply permission.

choices.text: End the meeting and send all three home, even if the recommendation disappears before morning.
choices.result_text:
{name} switched off the screen and told all three to go. The supervisor said he could not guarantee the post after his executive call. Minseo lifted her bag; Hyunsu hesitated, then left with them.

After the elevator carried them down, {name} remained alone. The shortcut through other people's evenings had closed, and the recommendation was no longer his to assume. Three empty chairs faced him from different angles, each holding a reason he would have to state alone tomorrow.

title: The Promise Before Authority
description:
Before the executive meeting, the supervisor brought {name} to an empty training room. Two teams waited beyond the glass. He stopped at its locked door. “Authority begins only when the appointment takes effect. Today, explain whose time your terms protect. Neither access card nor seat exists yet.”

{name} could surrender KRW 150,000 from the KRW 450,000 allowance, accept the final KRW 300,000, and preserve the temporary role; delay ten days for a handover; or cover missing nights under a smaller budget. The first path created only a spoken promise and an amended draft. Filing and execution still lay ahead.

Hyunsu and Minseo were absent, so their refusals could not certify him clean. The door stayed locked while {name} chose which cost to promise under his own name.

choices.text: Give up KRW 150,000 of the KRW 450,000 allowance, accept the final KRW 300,000, and explain the promise to preserve the temporary role.
choices.result_text:
Before both teams outside the glass, {name} explained that he would give up KRW 150,000 of the KRW 450,000 monthly allowance, accept the final KRW 300,000, and place the condition preserving the existing temporary role in the amended draft. The supervisor stayed at the locked door. “Less money does not make you a good manager. Today, you have only promised those words under your name.”

{name} did not enter the new-team room or assign any night work. No new badge was issued, and the manager's seat stayed empty until execution. The people had heard the condition but did not yet ask him for a start time. A promise now existed; its authority and cost waited beyond filing and execution.

choices.text: Delay the appointment ten days and guarantee both teams time to hand over their work themselves.
choices.result_text:
The supervisor erased the recommendation mark beside {name}'s name on the executive schedule. “I cannot promise this place is yours in ten days.” {name} still asked for the two teams to meet and explain their own work.

The people outside the training room began arranging a handover instead of dispersing. No one called {name} their manager that day. The teams gained time to speak; he lost the fastest executive window. The ten days remained not as calendar boxes, but as the place from which his recommendation had been withdrawn.

choices.text: Choose the twenty-percent budget cut, but refuse an appointment that removes the temporary role.
choices.result_text:
{name} chose the twenty-percent budget cut. The supervisor removed the temporary-role extension from his folder and told the worker waiting beyond the glass that the company could no longer ask them to report to this post. The worker peeled the temporary name card from the training-room wall and put it in a bag.

{name} neither promised to cover the vacancy with his nights nor assigned a team he did not lead. He said he would not proceed with the appointment on those terms. The supervisor folded the recommendation and removed his name from the executive list. The budget and one person's place shrank together; the manager path ended at the locked door.

title: The Blue Pen Between Two Doors
description:
The left door led to his current team; the right led to the new task-force room after the effective date. Employees clocked out behind {name} at the chained blue pen. A notice said filing was conditional, and no new badge existed.

Filing in his name fixed the terms, but {name} kept his desk and old badge until execution; the new seat, authority, and first promises waited. Withdrawal ended the recommendation. Giving up the deadline allowed an apology on Hyunsu's walk home without asking for an answer, but lost the appointment. Leaving unsigned made both teams wait.

Paper could hold conditions, not open a door. {name} chose whose name entered the filing and who waited for execution.

choices.text: Withdraw the appointment, return through the current-team door, and tell them the recommendation is over.
choices.result_text:
{name} put down the pen and withdrew. While the clerk collected the paper, he opened the left door. {name}'s current team stopped packing to look at him. He said first that he would share tomorrow's work, not that he had lost a promotion.

The supervisor arrived late and warned that the recommendation might never return. The new training-room door stayed closed. {name} recovered his familiar desk, but the opportunity and the gaze that had marked him as the next manager remained outside it.

choices.text: File conditionally under his own name and defer the new seat and first promises until execution.
choices.result_text:
{name} filed conditionally without another person's name. The clerk read the filed copy's final KRW 300,000 monthly allowance, preservation of the existing temporary role, and effective date, then returned it in an envelope. “Keep your current desk and badge until execution. You have no authority over the new team yet.” The right door remained locked.

{name} told the waiting people beyond the glass only that the filing had been received. He promised neither to take night work nor to decide anyone's departure time. They packed without pulling a chair forward. His name and both conditions were filed, but no new badge was issued; the new seat, manager authority, and first-week words all waited until execution.

choices.text: Give up the filing deadline, meet Hyunsu on his way home, and apologize in person for trying to borrow his name.
choices.result_text:
{name} put down the blue pen and told the clerk he would not file today. After the deadline closed, he went to the crosswalk behind the accounting firm as Hyunsu left night work. Hyunsu did not stop when he saw {name}. Keeping one pace back, {name} said, “I am not asking for your answer again. I came to apologize for placing your name ahead of my chance.”

Hyunsu waited until the light turned green. Across the street he said, “Not filing was your choice. Don't call it compensation for my refusal. But I heard the apology.” He walked toward the convenience store with room for one person beside him. {name} lost the appointment chance but no longer put Hyunsu's refusal inside a deadline. One block remained in which they might begin the next conversation.

choices.text: Leave unsigned, visit both teams, and ask them to wait until his answer tomorrow morning.
choices.result_text:
{name} set down the pen and stood first at his current team's threshold, then outside the new room's glass door. He gave both the same sentence: “I will not enter either door tonight. I will answer tomorrow morning.” The request to wait produced different faces beyond each door.

The supervisor assigned the empty night to someone else, and the new team packed up. {name} had not erased the decision, but tied two groups' evening to his hesitation. When the corridor lights went out, he alone stood between both doors.

title: The Person Who Did Not Come Down
description:
At the accounting firm's front desk, {name} arrived thirty minutes early with the appointment copy. Hyunsu replied from upstairs. “Hyung, I am not coming down today. Leave it at the desk. I'll read it and contact you first.”

{name} had come straight after work, keeping the evening empty so he could explain face to face that he had not used Hyunsu's name. Hyunsu owned the right not to hear that explanation and to choose when he answered. The receptionist could take the envelope; the elevator opened and closed, but Hyunsu never appeared.

Waiting would turn refusal into bargaining. Going upstairs crossed a workplace boundary. The copy could remain as a result, but the meeting was not {name}'s to claim. He had to respect the distance and leave without seeing Hyunsu.

choices.text: Respect Hyunsu's distance, leave the envelope at the front desk, and turn away without meeting him.
choices.result_text:
{name} gave the envelope to the receptionist, naming only the person who would receive it. He texted that he would not wait, then stepped back from the elevator. The floor numbers climbed above him, but he asked no door to open.

The thirty early minutes and round trip did not return, and he never saw Hyunsu's face. The copy could reach him; {name}'s explanation and apology could not enter the lobby with it. The revolving-door glass reflected only a man turning away alone. The distance until Hyunsu called first was not a date, but an empty space in their relationship.

title: The Name Left Behind the Blank Field
description:
At the late cafe, Hyunsu left his copy titled self-name filing closed and placed his firm badge face down. “Hyung, I saw that my name was left off the paper.”

{name} set out his filed copy and Minseo's blue-marked review sheet. Hyunsu drew the blue-marked end date closer. “While you calculated that my name made it five days, I didn't know what I would be recorded as reviewing. A firm name isn't lettering you erase. One wrong table could follow me into my next job.”

The ice before {name} had nearly melted. The clean field showing no external reviewer proved the filing state. It did not erase Hyunsu's time and professional boundary before that field was closed.

choices.text: Close the filed copy and hear Hyunsu to the end.
choices.result_text:
Hyunsu described where his time had gone, from the day his name was first raised to the lobby where he received the copy. “Not using it in the end was your choice, Hyung. The time I spent waiting for that choice was mine. Write down both.”

{name} kept his hand still on the filed copy. He waited for Hyunsu's sentence to end as the last ice melted. Hyunsu put the copy in his bag and set his cold glass on the return counter. One sheet for a next date stayed blank on the table.

choices.text: Explain first that the final filing did not use Hyunsu's name.
choices.result_text:
{name} pointed from the empty external-reviewer field to his own signature. Hyunsu looked at the sheet, then put his badge back around his neck. “I know the result. I'm asking why my name was a shortcut to you in the first place.”

The clean field became evidence in a rebuttal, and the conversation shortened. Hyunsu put the filed copy in his bag and stood. The note field for the date his name was first raised stayed blank before {name}.

choices.text: Ask Hyunsu to define the boundary sentence they should use from now on.
choices.result_text:
When {name} offered a blank notepad, Hyunsu did not take the pen. “If I write your company's rule too, you're putting my time in the review field again.”

He pressed only the empty external-reviewer field on his copy. “You write the next sentence. Ask me then if you need to—don't put my name up first.” The notepad returned blank to {name}. Hyunsu's boundary remained in the hand that had declined the pen.

title: Which Door Tomorrow
description:
Two doors stood beyond the counter. His team handed over on the left. The new room held two separate places: an empty manager chair for {name}, and the temporary worker's desk protected by the filed terms. The worker stood beside that desk, bag on one shoulder. The supervisor rested a hand between {name}'s worn badge and an empty reader. “One signature, one door tomorrow.”

Accepting brought KRW 300,000 monthly, twelve months' responsibility, and a KRW 6 million early-exit cost. Refusing kept his job but closed the recommendation; resigning ended salary and commute. Neither Hyunsu's refusal nor Minseo's lost evening made a path clean.

A new-team member asked what time to arrive. In the old room, someone waited with {name}'s drawer key. Their faces demanded an answer before the pen did.

choices.text: Accept the appointment, enter the new-team door, and state the first week's night promise to those waiting.
choices.result_text:
{name} accepted in his own name. When the new badge lit, he opened the right door. He told the waiting people that the first missing night duty would come to him, and that no one's departure would count as spare capacity. The temporary worker put the bag beneath their own chair and set the removed name card upright on their own desk.

From outside, the supervisor said, “Promises are easy today. A month from now is your responsibility.” The drawer key in the old room passed to someone else, while {name}'s jacket went over the new chair. The title and allowance arrived as the familiar way back closed. People asked about tomorrow's start, not congratulations.

choices.text: Refuse the appointment, return to his current team, and hear together that this recommendation is over.
choices.result_text:
{name} did not take the new badge. The supervisor said the recommendation ended this quarter and closed the task-force door. {name} returned through the left door, where the person holding his drawer key gave it back.

The current team folded the handover without relief or disappointment. Tomorrow's commute and salary remained, but the next post his supervisor had backed with his own name disappeared. After the closing announcement, the light behind the right door stayed on for another manager.

choices.text: Leave both appointment paths and resign from the authority and stability the company lent him.
choices.result_text:
{name} confirmed his resignation and removed the badge from his neck. Rather than plead, the supervisor read the remaining leave and final payday himself. “I don't know whether outside is freedom. This door closes today.”

Someone from the old team received the drawer key; someone from the new team pushed the nameless chair inside. {name} crossed the lobby through neither door. He lost next month's salary and the shelter of employment, but also left a life explained by authority the company could reclaim tomorrow. His hand felt strange without an employee pass.

title: Until the Night Bus Came
description:
Only night-bus passengers remained at the stop between the company and the accounting firm. Hyunsu saw {name}'s new badge without congratulating him. He put the appointment-copy envelope in his bag. “You didn't call me here to approve that, did you?” The company phoned: the new team's welcome dinner was still going.

Hyunsu's bus came in twenty minutes. Returning let {name} hear the first toast as manager. Staying shared the interval before Hyunsu went back to night work. Explaining the appointment or asking forgiveness would turn the stop into another meeting room.

“You decide now when people may go home, Hyung. Stay until the bus comes. Don't forget how long that is.” The envelope had arrived. The choice was losing the welcome dinner to stand beside that wait.

choices.text: Turn off the company call and wait beside Hyunsu, without explanation, until the night bus arrives.
choices.result_text:
{name} closed the new-team chat and stood beside Hyunsu. They spoke not about the appointment, but about late buses and the last light at the accounting firm. Hyunsu did not open the envelope, and {name} did not ask him to read it.

The supervisor never called again. In the first-dinner photo, {name}'s chair was empty. As the bus arrived, Hyunsu put one foot on the step. “Don't tell the team you repaid them because you waited today. Just remember.” Behind the closed bag and departing bus remained the first company night the new manager had lost.

title: Three Evenings at the Transfer Platform
description:
Turning thirty-eight in seven days, {name} stood on a transfer platform. His first approved half-day had just begun. The new task-force chat moved the executive review to tonight; the supervisor said {name} could return and speak his first result. Hyunsu held one seat at the old-neighborhood gukbap place until nine. The train home was arriving too.

Returning let {name} send the team home and own the report, but ended Hyunsu's meal and his leave. The restaurant kept a person's evening while the company remembered his result in another voice. Home preserved {name}'s first hours for himself in five years, while company and friend received his absence.

The appointment copy was in his bag. The new badge could not open all three doors. Only one body could enter one evening.

choices.text: Return to the company, send the team home, and speak the first result to the executives in his own voice.
choices.result_text:
{name} crossed to the opposite platform and opened the company door with his new badge. He sent the remaining team home, then sat alone before the screen. The supervisor connected the call and said, “From today, you chose this time.”

{name} spoke the first result and its failure himself. At nine, Hyunsu left the gukbap place without ordering, and the approved leave did not return. While gaining his voice inside the organization, he lost a person's evening and his own hours in the same night. The black screen reflected only empty team desks.

choices.text: Go to the gukbap place, keep the meal Hyunsu waited for, and let someone else carry the first company result.
choices.result_text:
{name} let the company train leave and went to the old goshiwon alley. Before the soup arrived, Hyunsu said, “If company talk comes first tonight, I leave.” {name} put the new badge in his pocket and listened to the nights Hyunsu protected now.

The executive review ended in the supervisor's and another manager's voices. Tomorrow the company would remember first that {name} was absent from his own result. Hyunsu's empty chair was filled, but the first chance to speak inside the organization and the rest of his leave were gone.

choices.text: Give the approved leave to no one, switch off the phone, and go home.
choices.result_text:
{name} sent one short message to the company and one to Hyunsu saying he would go to neither place, then turned off the phone. The train window held the edge of his new badge over his tired face. At home he shut off the alarm and lay down without turning on the light.

The executive review proceeded without him; Hyunsu pushed in the empty chair at nine. No one took {name}'s leave, but neither place lost the fact of waiting. Keeping one whole night for himself after five years left a morning in which both organization and friend remembered his absence.

title: The Glass Door and Twenty Minutes
description:
Beyond the glass wall of the acquirer's meeting room, office lights went dark one row at a time. The acquisition lead was polite but direct. “We're not buying only the code. We're buying the people who will still answer the phone tomorrow.” A live demonstration of the working service was due in twenty minutes. Sujin messaged that she was ready to connect; back at the office, the cofounder was making final checks with the team.

The lead wanted both founders to explain the company together. If both stayed in this room, the team and Sujin would carry the live service alone. If one returned, the buyer would remember the company through the voice that remained. The water before {name} was untouched, and the minute hand beyond the glass was already moving toward the next promise.

choices.text: Have {name} stay to explain the offer and demonstration alone, and send the cofounder back to the team.
choices.result_text:
The cofounder watched {name} for a moment, then rose. “I'll take the other side, then.” After the glass door closed, the lead asked the question again. {name} explained the company's beginning and what the acquisition would change.

Twenty minutes later the service appeared onscreen without the cofounder's voice. The lead listened to the end but promised no decision that day. The team got the cofounder back, and {name} kept control of his own stake's story. The company they had made together remained in the room as one person's sentence.

choices.text: Accept the cofounder's offer to explain the company and service, and have {name} return to Sujin.
choices.result_text:
The cofounder pulled the empty water glass closer. “Go to the customer. I'll tell them here why we came this far.” {name} nodded and left through the glass door.

When he joined the office screen, Sujin immediately pointed out the service's slow section. At the same time, the cofounder answered the acquirer's questions about the company and service. The live service regained both of their hands, but {name} never heard the full story told about the company they had made together.

choices.text: Keep both founders with the buyer, leaving the team and Sujin to run the demonstration and live service.
choices.result_text:
{name} told Sujin that both founders would be absent. Her reply was short: “Then we'll start with the team.” The cofounder turned their phone facedown, and the two founders sat side by side before the lead.

The demonstration began on time. Inside the room, the founders described the same company's future; outside it, the team and Sujin carried the questions and the live trouble. The lead listened carefully but promised neither acceptance nor success. The founders preserved their joint authorship, while people outside the room paid the service's next twenty minutes.

title: A Cold Second Meal and a Third Chair
description:
A third chair was tucked beneath the café table. Minseo's soup had been reheated twice and gone cold again; the cofounder had come straight from the office without taking off their coat. Before {name} sat, Minseo drew a boundary. “I'm not the person who approves this deal or gives you legal clearance. Don't turn the fact that I checked the arithmetic into my permission.”

The cofounder did not discuss the price either. “I didn't come to get {name}'s price approved. I came to say what kind of Monday we'll have to live.” Team alerts gathered on the phone, and a buyer-preparation call waited an hour away. Neither person offered {name} a blessing. The cold bowl and the tucked chair said only that he had not yet taken the seat where he had to listen.

choices.text: Pull out the third chair, hear the cofounder to the end, then walk toward the office with them.
choices.result_text:
{name} pulled the chair from under the table and dismissed the buyer-call alert. The cofounder began with the empty seats the team would see next Monday. Minseo did not build an answer for him. Café light trembled once over the cold soup.

By the time all three stepped outside, the preparation call had passed. {name} walked with them as far as the lane leading back to the customer and office. No one had approved the sale, and he could not lean on their opposition either. He lost the hour he had tried to protect, while the cofounder's Monday stayed in his ears from first sentence to last.

title: The Dark Pitch Screen and the Open Door
description:
When the acquisition lead sat down in the startup's small office, the team stopped working and turned on the pitch screen. Then Sujin appeared at the door. She had left work and traveled across the city without closing the live service on her hot laptop. When she opened the screen that was still running, one team member switched off the polished presentation on the wall. The slow moment the customer had just endured took its place.

The acquisition lead closed the door against the hall noise; the cofounder immediately opened it again. Outside stood the team whose work had stopped. Inside, there was one empty chair. Sujin could not stay much longer, and the lead had another meeting. No one continued until {name} decided who would be treated as a guest in this room.

choices.text: Leave the door the cofounder reopened as it is, and give Sujin {name}'s chair.
choices.result_text:
{name} took his hand from the doorknob and pushed his chair toward Sujin. The acquisition lead shifted closer to the wall. The cofounder stood between the open door and the team. When Sujin sat, the hot laptop's fan filled the room for a moment.

The team outside did not disperse back to work; their time had already stopped. {name} alone remained standing as they watched Sujin's screen. The pitch had ended, and the deal had not begun. The reason a customer had come in person and the questions the team had not asked now occupied the same room. Who would be made to wait next could no longer be avoided.

title: One Hour Outside the Door
description:
Inside the open door, Sujin turned the live service toward {name}. “Who do we call next time it stops?” The cofounder looked at the team. No one could promise a name for the people who would remain after the acquisition. The team stood between the hall and meeting room, their work stopped. Sujin had stayed beyond the time she could spare.

The acquisition lead reopened the laptop: an internal decision that day required the meeting to continue. It was fact, not a threat. Opening the room to everyone would cost the deal its speed; continuing would push the team and Sujin's questions outside. If {name} left with Sujin, the cofounder would carry the company-and-service questions while he lost sight of the acquisition discussion. The hour did not pass equally for them.

choices.text: Ask the acquisition lead to wait outside for one hour, and hear the team and Sujin's questions.
choices.result_text:
The acquisition lead checked the time, picked up the laptop, and stepped into the hall. “I can't promise that a decision today will still be possible in an hour.” While the lead made a call beyond the open door, the team asked why they had learned so late. Sujin asked again whom she should call during the next failure.

An hour later, the lead had left for the next meeting. {name} lost the day's speed and its chance at approval. He had not solved the team or Sujin's questions. He had only refused to take away the time they needed to finish asking them. Sujin's warm handprint remained on the chair where the buyer's laptop had been.

choices.text: Keep the acquisition lead in the room and continue the sale discussion.
choices.result_text:
{name} turned the laptop back toward the acquisition lead. The cofounder asked the team to wait a little longer, and the meeting returned to price and future roles. Sujin rose without closing the live service. “We'll work out whom to call again ourselves.”

Sujin left first, and the team returned to their desks. The acquisition lead finished the necessary questions but guaranteed no acceptance that day. The room gained time for the deal. Outside it, the customer's question and the team's chance to ask their own questions closed together.

choices.text: Have {name} leave with Sujin, leaving the cofounder with the team and acquisition lead.
choices.result_text:
{name} lifted Sujin's laptop and left through the open door with her. In the descending elevator, she said her side would try to hold out alone during the next failure. It sounded less like reassurance than a refusal to keep waiting.

Back at the office, the cofounder took the team's questions and the acquisition lead's questions about the company and service at once. {name} went with the customer but lost the place from which he could watch the acquisition discussion turn. The cofounder carried the weight of both rooms. Their face did not appear in the closing elevator doors.

title: The Key on the Desk at Dawn
description:
After a long night, only the corridor light remained on. The cofounder placed their key and name badge on {name}'s desk. It looked like a departure, but the decision was more exact. “I'll stay through the current customer's handover and the first Monday after the acquisition. You don't get to decide my future after that.”

It was neither a request for protection nor permission to sell. The cofounder chose the remaining time they would carry for the team and customer, then took back the job and life that followed. If {name} pushed the key back or held it down, he would choose that boundary for them too. On the desk where they had begun together, the distance left in their relationship was the width of one key and one name badge.

choices.text: Leave the key and name badge untouched, and hear the cofounder's decision without stepping inside it.
choices.result_text:
{name} lowered the hand he had begun to extend. He did not say that staying longer would be safer or that leaving now would hurt less. The cofounder finished, in their own words, what they would protect through the customer handover and the first Monday.

Dawn reached the office while the key and badge stayed between them. The cofounder's work and future did not become part of the transaction, but the founders' relationship was not repaired either. What remained with {name} was a silence that had not chosen for someone else, and the last stretch of time they would still have to spend in the same office.

title: Words Late by One Empty Chair
description:
That afternoon, the cofounder stood among the team's desks and told them the decision directly. They would stay through the current customer's handover and the first Monday after the acquisition, but would not give the future beyond that to either company yet. It was a voice that had asked no one else to speak for it.

The question from the team came at once. “Why do we always hear when the decision is almost over?” Work screens went dark one by one as people surrendered more of their own time to hear an answer. There was no prepared place for {name}. One empty chair, normally used by someone else, remained among the team. Standing at the front would turn their question into another briefing. Sitting meant hearing what the people told too late had already lost.

choices.text: Sit in the empty chair among the team and hear the exchange with the cofounder to the end.
choices.result_text:
{name} sat among the people rather than before them. The cofounder took responsibility for speaking late without turning it into an excuse. The team asked about the seats they would occupy next Monday, who would go to Sujin, and whether they would have time to choose. {name} stopped himself from adding an answer and stayed seated until the questions ended.

The team had already lost an hour of the evening. No one said it was all right, and the cofounder did not forgive {name} on their behalf. The empty chair slid back beneath the desk. The time spent waiting by people who had learned late did not return to that day's work.

title: An Hour Beside the Customer's Screen
description:
On a small table inside Sujin's workplace, the work screen she would need again on Monday remained blocked and lit. Sujin stepped away from her work for an hour and seated both founders before it. Other people at the workplace divided her work among them, while the startup team kept the service running in place of this visit.

“We've been calling two people, not a company name.” Sujin turned the blocked screen toward {name}. “Don't answer for the future of a company that may be sold. I want to see which of you will be beside this screen if it stops again on Monday.” The cofounder sat silently beside her. Before a promise about the future, the moment needed time spent crossing one step where the customer had actually stopped.

choices.text: Sit beside Sujin and the cofounder, and move through the blocked screen's next step together.
choices.result_text:
{name} did not begin by saying who would come after the deal. He first asked where Sujin had stopped and how long she had waited in that state. The cofounder checked only the service as it existed now. The three stayed in place until the screen moved to its next step.

Sujin's lost hour and the time covered by the team did not return. One moving screen did not solve Monday either. {name} watched Sujin take the next step without promising the future, then rose. As he left for the final deal, the screen that had refused to move remained clearer in his eyes than the price.

title: The Alert Before the Transfer
description:
In the acquirer's closing room, the lead was about to transfer KRW 3.2 billion for {name}'s 20% stake. The lead calmly explained the one transition meeting after the deal and the line that would be hard to cross back over that day. Then Sujin's service alert sounded on both founders' phones.

The cofounder checked the screen and stood. “I'm going to the customer. Your twenty percent is yours to decide.” The lead did not stop them, only said leaving would close that day's transfer window. If {name} stayed, the money would move while his last independent response and founder's path went out the door. If he left, he would keep his stake, but no one promised the same chance again. {name}'s chair remained between the closing door and lit alert.

choices.text: Stay in the room and finish the sale.
choices.result_text:
The alert sounded once more after the cofounder left. {name} turned his phone facedown and answered the acquisition lead's final question. A bank alert appeared a moment later, and the access he had used as a founder ended. The lead gave the time of the one transition meeting after the acquisition but promised no success.

Beyond the glass door, the cofounder's chair was empty. {name} had sold his stake and crossed a line he could not retrace. His last response as an independent founder, and the road on which the two of them might have left together as independent founders, closed as the price of remaining in the room.

choices.text: Leave the room and go to the cofounder and Sujin.
choices.result_text:
When {name} stood, the acquisition lead took a hand from the confirmation button. “Today's window closes here. I can't promise the same terms again.” There was no anger in the voice. The lead simply closed the screen.

{name} took the stairs before the elevator arrived. His stake remained his, but the money available that day and the road beyond the acquisition were gone. When he reached the cofounder and Sujin, the alert was still active. No one asked first about the money he had left behind.

title: The Empty Place in the Elevator Mirror
description:
After the transfer, {name} stood alone before the elevator outside the closing room. In the mirror, the chair he had just left empty seemed clearer than the face of someone who had gained something new. He called the cofounder. The team and Sujin had already settled the alert, and the cofounder was still at Sujin's workplace.

The first question was not about the money. “Will you come hear for yourself what Sujin said at the end?” Through the call came coworkers returning to their work and the scrape of a chair. Even if {name} went now, he could not restore the alert he had missed or the time other people had paid in his place. The elevator doors opened. Inside lay the acquirer's transition appointment; behind him, the people of a night that had already ended.

choices.text: Let the elevator go, and head to where the cofounder and Sujin are.
choices.result_text:
As the doors closed, {name} stepped back. By the time he reached Sujin's workplace, both of them had moved beyond the blocked screen and closed the laptop. {name} did not explain his lateness with the price. He sat in the empty chair beside them.

Sujin spoke less about the moment the failure ended than the moment they had stopped waiting and moved first. The cofounder did not soften it for {name}. Time that money could not restore remained between the three of them. Unable to say he had repaid it, {name} listened through the last words of a night already over and turned off the light with them.

title: Three Doors Closing in One Night
description:
Seven days before his thirty-eighth birthday, Seoul's night doubled in the old startup office windows. A notebook lay open: “Age thirty-three. Cash: KRW 500,000.” Three doors would close that evening. The team held {name}'s place at its last independent dinner. The cofounder would spend the current customer's night with Sujin, leaving a chair by the blocked screen. The acquirer reserved him a seat at a one-off transition dinner.

All began together. The team wanted a shared meal, not a speech. Sujin wanted to see a face before Monday's operation. The acquisition lead said the transition talk would start without {name}. Choosing one place put his absence in the other two. Five years had taught {name} money could not lengthen time. Only three directions remained.

choices.text: Stay for the team's last dinner as an independent company.
choices.result_text:
{name} turned off the old office lights with the team and went to the small restaurant. The cofounder's chair was empty, and the place Sujin had held beside the blocked screen never received him. The team told stories about meals they had missed across five years, and {name} heard laughter available only at that table.

At the same time, the acquirer's transition dinner began with other people's voices. The cofounder and Sujin faced Monday's customer operation without him. Neither empty place filled when the meal ended. {name} gained the team's last dinner. The other two doors did not reopen that night.

choices.text: Go to the customer's night where the cofounder and Sujin are waiting.
choices.result_text:
{name} went to Sujin's workplace and sat beside the cofounder before Monday's service check. The three shared cold coffee in silence before they opened the blocked screen. When Sujin called both founders' names, both answered her that night.

At the team's restaurant, {name}'s and the cofounder's chairs remained empty side by side. The acquirer's transition dinner also began without him. A late team photo showed two untouched plates. In exchange for the customer's night, he lost the last independent dinner and the buyer's transition table. Neither promised another chance.

choices.text: Take the seat at the acquirer's transition dinner.
choices.result_text:
{name} passed through a glass door in the opposite direction from the old office and took the reserved chair. The acquisition lead began the one-off transition discussion. No one congratulated his choice or promised the company would thrive after the acquisition. The people at this table did not know the two places he had just left empty.

{name}'s phone showed a photo from the team's last dinner, then a short missed call from Sujin. The photo held {name}'s empty plate; the customer's workplace held the unused chair. While he took the buyer's transition seat, the independent company's last night and the current customer's time closed without him.
